To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) viral decline during triple therapy with sofosbubir + GS-9669 + ledispar, sofosbuvur + GS9451 + ledispavir and sofosbuvuir + ledipsavir was slow, 2) viral kinetics did not explain the rapid cure observed with these treatments, 3) a model incorporating drug effects on virus infectivity was necessary to explain the rapid cure, 4)
the paradoxical rapid cure observed with sofosbubir-based combination therapies is due to the generation of non-infectious virions, which can be predicted with a mathematical model.

“The rapid cure rate achieved by sofosbuvr-based triple therapy is disconnected from the slow viral kinetics and is likely due to the rapid generation of non-infectious viral particles by the NS5A or protease-inhibition”.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mathematical modelling of viral infection dynamics in the presence of antiviral treatment.
understanding the mechanisms underlying the rapid cure rates achieved with new direct acting antiviral agents (DAA), and the possibility of reducing treatment duration further.
mathematical modelling of the dynamics of viral infections and the effects of antiviral drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the viral kinetics observed in the study are slow, but the SVR rates observed are fast, and that the paradox can be resolved by assuming that the drug combinations generate non-infective virions.

the viral kinetics observed are not sufficient to explain the high SVR rate achieved with the new drugs, and that a model including the effect of drugs in generating non-infective virus is needed to explain the high cure rates.
the rapid cure rate is disconnected from the virus load measurements during treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
viral load measurements are not a reliable indicator of cure for patients receiving sofosbuvur-based triple therapy.
we need a new way to measure the effect of anti-HCV therapy.
the rapid cure observed with the new direct antiviral agents (DAAs) is not due to the viral load reduction during treatment but to the generation of non-infectious particles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the viral kinetics observed in patients treated with sofosbivir and ledipasvir do not explain the high cure rates observed in these studies.
we cannot predict SVR rates from viral load measurements during treatment.
we should not rely on viral loads measured during the treatment when predicting cure rates.
